passage:
"I'm not going to Chaitanya's birthday," Pradeep announced, dropping his bag.
Amma looked up from the vegetables. "Since when?"
"Since today. He laughed when I missed the penalty. In front of everyone. He's a fake friend. Always has been."
"Always?"
"Always."
"The Chaitanya who sat with you every day when you broke your arm in Class 6?"
Pradeep paused. "That was ages ago."
"The one who shared his notes before the exams? Who came at midnight when Thatha was in hospital?"
"...He still laughed today."
"He did. That was mean, and you can tell him so. But is today the whole story of him?"
Pradeep kicked at the doormat. "It feels like it."

qa.q: When did Pradeep break his arm?
qa.a: In Class 6.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep call Chaitanya a fake friend who "always has been"?
qa.a: Today's laugh hurts and is the freshest memory, so it feels like the truth about Chaitanya and pushes years of kindness out of view.

qa.q: What does Amma suggest Pradeep can do about the laugh?
qa.a: Tell Chaitanya it was mean, rather than dropping the friendship, while remembering today isn't the whole story.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel if Pradeep skipped the birthday without a word?
qa.a: Chaitanya might be confused and hurt, perhaps without even realising how much the laugh stung.

grounding: It shows a teenager judging a long-time friend by the latest quarrel and forgetting years of kindness.

passage: Last month I almost blocked Sumit. We'd had a stupid fight over our chemistry project: he forgot the chart paper, I snapped, he snapped back, and he said I always act like the boss. That night all I could think was, "That's who Sumit really is. Careless and rude." I'm Mridul, and I've known Sumit since we were six. He taught me to ride a cycle. He stood up for me when some seniors mocked my stammer in Class 7. He once walked me home in the rain when I was sick. None of that came into my head that night, only the chart paper and "boss". My sister asked, "Is he really like that, or was he like that today?" It took me a week to answer.

qa.q: What did Sumit forget?
qa.a: The chart paper.

qa.q: Why did Mridul think that night that Sumit was "careless and rude"?
qa.a: Mridul felt angry after the fight, the most recent thing between them, so it seemed like the real Sumit, and years of kindness like the cycle and the stammer didn't come to mind.

qa.q: What does the sister's question help Mridul see?
qa.a: The difference between one bad day and who Sumit has been for years, so a single fight doesn't decide the whole friendship.

qa.q: What might Sumit have felt during that week?
qa.a: Sumit might have been hurt by the fight too, and unsure whether a friendship going back to age six was over.

grounding: It shows a teenager treating the latest fight as the truth about a friend and forgetting years of kindness.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9B, Friday.
Shalini asked this morning to be moved away from Kavitha. They have sat together since Class 5. Yesterday they argued over a shared lunch box that was left open and ants got in; I heard raised voices. Shalini told me, "She's always been selfish, ma'am. I just didn't see it." When I asked for another example, she couldn't give one. Then she remembered, on her own, that Kavitha had brought her notes every day when she was ill for weeks last year, and she went quiet. I have not moved the seat yet. I suggested they each tell the other one thing they were upset about, with me nearby if they want. I'll check with both on Monday.

qa.q: How long have Shalini and Kavitha sat together?
qa.a: Since Class 5.

qa.q: Why does Shalini say Kavitha has "always been selfish"?
qa.a: Yesterday's argument is fresh and hurts, so it feels like the real Kavitha, even though Shalini can't name another example.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking for another example let Shalini remember Kavitha's kindness on her own, and not moving the seat yet gave the friendship a chance.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel if she learned Shalini wanted to change seats?
qa.a: Kavitha might feel shocked and hurt that one argument over a lunch box outweighed years of sitting together and bringing notes.

grounding: It shows a teenager judging a long-time friend by one recent quarrel and forgetting her past kindness.

passage:
Saturday night
Raghav and I are DONE. Today at the science exhibition he told Ma'am that the solar oven idea was his. It was OURS. I did the foil and the angles. He just stood there nodding while she praised him.
I told him in the corridor he's a selfish show-off. He said I'm "always so dramatic". So that's it. He's always been like this, I just never saw it.
Mumma said, "Raghav, beti? The boy who walked you home every day in Class 5 when you were scared of the dogs?" And that he gave me half his tiffin for a whole month when mine got stolen.
I know. But that was ages ago. Today is what he's REALLY like.
Deleting his number tomorrow.
— Vidya

qa.q: What did Raghav tell Ma'am at the science exhibition?
qa.a: He told Ma'am that the solar oven idea was his.

qa.q: Why does today's quarrel feel like the truth about Raghav to Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya is freshly hurt, so the latest event feels like his real character, and the years of walking home together and sharing tiffin seem like they no longer count.

qa.q: At which moment could Vidya choose differently, and what might she do?
qa.a: Before deleting his number tomorrow; she could wait a few days, think about the Class 5 walks and the shared tiffin, and then tell Raghav calmly that she wants credit for her part.

qa.q: How might Raghav be feeling after being called a selfish show-off?
qa.a: Raghav may feel stung and defensive, as his "dramatic" comeback suggests, and perhaps a bit guilty if he knows he took too much credit.

passage: Sharmila slammed the door of her room in their Hyderabad flat and threw her bag on the bed. Keerthana had told the whole project team that Sharmila's slides were "messy". In front of everyone! "She's always been like this," Sharmila told her mother through the door. "Selfish. Showing off." That night, hunting for a charger in her drawer, she found a crumpled card: 'Get well soon, I'll bring your notes every day. K.' Class 7, when she'd been ill for a month. Under it lay a friendship band from Class 8 and a photo of the two of them at Keerthana's cousin's wedding, dancing badly. Sharmila sat on the floor holding them. 'Always like this' didn't fit. One mean comment today; years of notes, bands and bad dancing before it. She picked up her phone and typed, 'Can we talk tomorrow?'

qa.a: Keerthana told the whole project team that Sharmila's slides were 'messy'.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila feel sure that Keerthana had 'always been like this'?
qa.a: Sharmila felt angry and humiliated, and the fresh quarrel felt like the whole truth about Keerthana, crowding out years of kindness.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that was wise, and what could she do tomorrow?
qa.a: She let the old card, band and photo remind her of the whole friendship before acting; tomorrow she could tell Keerthana how the comment hurt and listen too.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the quarrel?

"I'm done with Gargi. Done."
"What happened now?" Didi looked up from her laptop.
"She didn't save me a seat on the trip bus. She sat with the new girl the whole way to the waterfall. She's fake. She never cared."
"Never?"
"Never."
"The Gargi who sat with you in the hospital when you broke your arm? Who has made you that terrible cake every birthday since Class 4?"
"That was ages ago."
"Last March is ages ago?"
Tejas picked at the sofa cushion. "It still felt like she didn't care today."
"Today, maybe. Not never. Did you ask her why?"
"No."
"Maybe the new girl had no one to sit with."
Tejas was quiet. Then he picked up his phone. "I'll ask. But I'm still annoyed."
"That's allowed."

qa.a: The trip bus was going to the waterfall.

qa.q: Why did Tejas decide that Gargi 'never cared'?
qa.a: Tejas felt hurt and left out on the bus, and that fresh sting felt like the truth about Gargi, pushing out the hospital visit and the birthday cakes.

qa.q: What small step did Didi push Tejas towards, and why?
qa.a: Asking Gargi why she sat with the new girl, because the latest quarrel might have a simple reason that fits with years of kindness.

qa.q: Why might Gargi have sat with the new girl?
qa.a: The new girl may have had no one to sit with, so Gargi might have been being kind rather than rejecting Tejas.

passage: Last winter I almost ended a six-year friendship over one afternoon. I'm Asif. Tejas and I had been best friends since Class 4. That afternoon, at the colony cricket final, Tejas ran me out, on purpose I thought, and laughed. I walked off the ground and blocked Tejas's number that night. For a week I told everyone Tejas had always been jealous of me. I really believed it. Then Ammi asked me who had stayed on the phone with me every night when Abbu was in hospital. Tejas. Who had lent me a bat when mine broke, and never asked for it back? Tejas. I sat there, stomach twisting. One run-out, and I had rewritten six years. I unblocked the number and called. Tejas said sorry first.

qa.q: Since which class had Asif and Tejas been best friends?
qa.a: They had been best friends since Class 4.

qa.q: Why did Asif believe Tejas had always been jealous?
qa.a: Asif felt humiliated and angry about the run-out and the laugh, and that recent moment felt like the truth about the whole friendship.

qa.q: Which question from Ammi changed things, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking who had stayed on the phone every night when Abbu was in hospital, because it brought back years of kindness that one afternoon had crowded out.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt during the week of being blocked?
qa.a: Tejas was probably confused and sad, cut off by a best friend of six years over one run-out.

grounding: Shows a teenager rewriting a long friendship around one recent quarrel until reminded of years of kindness.

passage:
School counsellor's note, 22 July.
Kamal came to see me, upset. He says he is done with his friend Naveen. On Monday, Naveen laughed when Kamal fell during football and didn't help him up. "He's a bad friend. He always was."
I asked Kamal to tell me about Naveen from before Monday. It took him a while. Naveen had sat with him every day when his grandfather died last year. Naveen had shared his notes before every exam since Class 6. Naveen had defended him when older boys teased him.
Kamal went quiet. "But Monday felt like the real him," he said. I said Monday was real, and so were the six years.
He has agreed to talk to Naveen and tell him the laugh hurt. We will meet again next week.

qa.q: What did Naveen do on Monday that upset Kamal?
qa.a: Naveen laughed when Kamal fell during football and didn't help him up.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry, sure that the latest quarrel showed Naveen's true self.

qa.q: What did the counsellor help Kamal do, and what is his next step?
qa.a: Recall six years of Naveen's kindness alongside Monday; his next step is to talk to Naveen and say the laugh hurt.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel if Kamal suddenly ended the friendship?
qa.a: Naveen would likely feel confused and hurt, having been a loyal friend for years before one careless laugh.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager judging a friend by the latest hurt and forgetting years of kindness.

Thursday night.
Rukmini didn't save me a seat at the farewell today. She sat with the new girls. I'm Pranav, and I'm so angry. I think she was never really my friend. I'm going to stop talking to her.
Friday night.
Couldn't sleep, so I looked through my old photos. Rukmini at my birthday in Class 6, holding the cake. Rukmini at the hospital when I broke my leg in Class 8, with comics. Rukmini staying back to help me with my science model, until seven.
One seat. Six years of this.
Maybe she didn't even see me come in. Maybe the new girls asked her. I don't know. But one seat isn't the whole story.
I'll ask her tomorrow instead of ignoring her.

qa.a: She may not have seen Pranav come in, or the new girls may have asked her, without meaning to hurt anyone.

In the small town of Wai, Omkar and Noor had been friends since they could walk. Noor had shared tiffin with him every day of Class 3, when his mother was in hospital. Noor had stayed up the night before his board exam, quizzing him on dates.
On Tuesday, Noor returned Omkar's cycle with a flat tyre and said, "It was already soft, yaar." Omkar shouted. Noor shouted back and walked off.
All week Omkar told everyone, "Noor's selfish. Always has been." As he said it, he believed it completely.
On Saturday his mother found an old photo: two small children under the neem tree, sharing one plate of poha. "Always selfish?" she asked.
Omkar looked at the photo for a long time. Then he fixed the tyre himself and wheeled the cycle over to Noor's house.

qa.a: Omkar felt angry and hurt after Tuesday's quarrel, and that fresh fight felt like the whole truth about Noor.

qa.q: What could Omkar do before judging a friend after a fight?
qa.a: Omkar could remember the long record, like the shared tiffin and the night of quizzing, before deciding who someone really is.

On Friday, at the school concert in Rotterdam, Noa didn't save Nkechi a seat. Nkechi stood at the back for the whole first half, and when she finally found Noa at the interval, Noa was laughing with the new girls from the hockey team.
"Thanks for nothing," Nkechi said, and left early.
All weekend she lay on her bed deciding Noa was fake, had always been fake, had probably only been friends with her out of pity.
On Sunday evening her brother dumped a box of old things on her bed while clearing the attic. Inside: a card Noa had made when Nkechi broke her arm in Year 7, covered in drawn plasters. A bracelet Noa had braided. Four years of notes passed in maths.
Nkechi held the card for a long time. One Friday against four years. She picked up her phone. "Can we talk?"

qa.q: Where did Nkechi stand for the first half of the concert?
qa.a: Nkechi stood at the back for the whole first half.

qa.q: Why did Nkechi decide Noa had always been fake?
qa.a: Nkechi felt hurt and left out after Friday, and the fresh sting made one bad evening feel like the truth about the whole friendship.

qa.q: What helped Nkechi see the friendship more fairly?
qa.a: The box of old things, the card, the bracelet and four years of notes, put the whole history beside one Friday.

qa.a: Noa may not have realised Nkechi had no seat, and could be confused and hurt by 'thanks for nothing'.

passage:
In the chemistry lab, with ten minutes left in the practical exam, Mohit knocked over the beaker. Their titration, three careful readings, soaked into the bench.
"You always ruin things!" Sarita hissed. Mohit's face went red. He didn't answer.
All week she avoided him in the corridor. When the class teacher asked her to choose a partner for the next project, she said, "Anyone but Mohit."
The teacher looked at her. "Didn't Mohit help you catch up when you missed a month in Class 9? And lend you his notes before every test since?"
Sarita opened her mouth. It was true. All of it. Three years of it, sitting behind one wet bench.
"One beaker," the teacher said, "and three years."
Sarita went to find Mohit at the water cooler.

qa.q: How many minutes were left when the beaker fell?
qa.a: Ten minutes were left in the practical exam.

qa.q: Why did Sarita say 'anyone but Mohit'?
qa.a: Sarita felt angry and let down after the spilled beaker, and that recent moment outweighed years of Mohit's help.

qa.q: What reminder from the teacher helped, and why?
qa.a: Recalling how Mohit helped Sarita catch up in Class 9 and lent notes before every test put three years next to one mistake.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt when Sarita hissed at him?
qa.a: Mohit was probably embarrassed and hurt, already upset about the beaker and then blamed as someone who always ruins things.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a lab partner by one recent mistake and forgetting years of kindness.

Dear Nisha didi,
Happy Christmas! Sorry this letter is so grumpy.
Zeenat and I are finished. On Friday she laughed when I tripped on stage during the carol programme, in front of everyone. That's who she really is: mean. I don't know how I never saw it before.
Okay, she did sit with me every lunch in class six when nobody else would. And she stayed on the phone with me the whole night Dadi was in hospital. And she made me that card for my thirteenth birthday with forty tiny drawings. But Friday is the real Zeenat. People show their true face eventually, right?
Mummy says I should sleep on it. I don't want to.
Write back and tell me I'm right.
Sarika

qa.a: Sleep on it as Mummy says, then tell Zeenat how the laugh felt, weighing Friday against the lunches, the phone call and the birthday card.

qa.a: Zeenat would probably feel hurt and shocked that one laugh erased years of sitting together at lunch and staying up on the phone.
